en: Theravāda Vinayapiṭaka Mahāvagga 6.
Bhesajjakkhandhaka (The Chapter on Medicines)
1. Discourse on the Five Medicines At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the bhikkhus were afflicted by an autumnal illness; even when they drank rice-gruel, it would come back up, and even when they ate solid food, it would come back up.
Because of that, they became emaciated, coarse, discolored, and jaundiced, with their limbs covered in a network of veins.
The Blessed One saw those bhikkhus who were emaciated, coarse, discolored, jaundiced, and whose limbs were covered in a network of veins; having seen them, he addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
"Ānanda, why are the bhikkhus now so emaciated, coarse, discolored, jaundiced, and with their limbs covered in a network of veins?"
“Venerable sir, at present, when the bhikkhus are afflicted by an autumnal illness, even the gruel they drink comes back up, and even the food they eat comes back up.
Because of this, they have become emaciated, haggard, discolored, and jaundiced, with their veins showing all over their limbs.
Then, while the Blessed One was alone in seclusion, this reflection arose in his mind:
“Now, at this time, when the monks are afflicted by the autumnal disease, even the rice-gruel they drink comes back up, and even the food they eat comes back up.
Because of that, they become emaciated, haggard, discolored, and jaundiced, with their limbs covered in a network of veins.

What medicinal treatment should I now authorize for the monks, which would be both a medicine and regarded as such by the world, which would serve the purpose of nutriment, yet would not be perceived as coarse food?”
Then it occurred to the Blessed One:
"There are these five tonics, namely:
ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey, and molasses."
“These medicines and those things considered as medicines by the world provide nourishment, yet no coarse food is perceived.
What if I were to allow these five medicines for the monks, to be accepted at the proper time and consumed at the proper time?
Then, in the evening, the Blessed One emerged from seclusion and, having given a Dhamma talk on this occasion and in this context, addressed the monks:
“Here, monks, while I was alone in seclusion, this reflection arose in my mind:
‘At present, when the monks are afflicted by an autumnal illness, even the rice-gruel they drink comes back up, and even the food they eat comes back up.
Because of that, they become emaciated, haggard, discolored, and jaundiced, with their limbs covered in visible veins.’”

“What medicinal treatment, then, might I allow for the monks that would be both a medicine and regarded as such by the world, which would serve the purpose of food yet would not be reckoned as gross food?
Then, monks, this occurred to me:
“There are these five medicines, namely:”
"Ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey, and molasses—these are medicines and what are recognized as medicines by the world; they serve the purpose of food, yet no coarse food is perceived.
What if I were to allow these five medicines for the bhikkhus, to be received at the proper time and consumed at the proper time?"
“I allow you, monks, to accept those five kinds of medicinal tonics at the proper time and consume them at the proper time.
Now at that time, the monks accepted those five kinds of medicinal tonics at the proper time and consumed them at the proper time;
yet even their ordinary, coarse foods did not satisfy them, let alone delicacies.

Afflicted by that very autumn illness and by this deprivation of food, they became even more emaciated, haggard, discolored, and jaundiced by both conditions, their limbs covered with a network of veins.
The Blessed One saw those bhikkhus who were even more emaciated, haggard, discolored, and jaundiced, their limbs covered with a network of veins; having seen them, he addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
“Ānanda, why is it that nowadays the bhikkhus are even more emaciated, coarse, discolored, sallow, and their limbs are so covered with veins?
“Venerable sir, at present the bhikkhus accept those five tonics at the proper time and consume them at the proper time.
Even those ordinary, coarse foods they eat do not satisfy them, let alone delicacies.”
“Afflicted by that very autumnal illness and by this lack of food and clothing, they became even more emaciated, haggard, discolored, jaundiced, and their limbs were covered with visible veins.
Then, on this occasion and in this context, the Blessed One gave a discourse on the Dhamma and addressed the bhikkhus:
“I allow you, bhikkhus, having received those five kinds of medicine, to consume them both at the proper time and at the improper time.”
Now at that time, sick monks had need of medicinal fats.
They informed the Blessed One of this matter.
"I allow you, monks, medicinal fats:—
Cow fat, fish fat, porpoise fat, pig fat, and donkey fat—
if received at the proper time, cooked at the proper time, and mixed at the proper time— it may be used for the purpose of oil.
But if, monks, it were received at an improper time, cooked at an improper time, and mixed at an improper time, and one were to use it, there is an offense of wrong-doing for three [acts].

“Monks, if one has received [food] at the proper time, and it is cooked at an improper time and mixed with [other food] at an improper time, and one should consume it, there is an offense of two *dukkaṭas*.
Monks, if one has received [food] at the proper time, and it is cooked at the proper time but mixed with [other food] at an improper time, and one should consume it, there is an offense of *dukkaṭa*.
Monks, if one has received [food] at the proper time, and it is cooked at the proper time and mixed with [other food] at the proper time, and one should consume it, there is no offense.”
2. Discussion on Root Medicines.
Now at that time, the sick monks had need of medicines made from roots.
They informed the Blessed One of this matter.
“I allow, monks, root medicines:
turmeric, ginger, sweet flag, *vacatta*, ativiṣa, bitter rohiṇī, usīra, and *bhaddamuttaka*;
or whatever other root medicines there may be that do not serve as food for the purpose of eating.”
They do not distribute what is edible for the purpose of edibility; rather,
having received them, they may keep them for as long as life lasts and consume them when there is a suitable occasion.
“There is an offense of wrong-doing for one who consumes [it] when there is no requisite.
Now at that time, sick monks had need of medicines made from roots and flour.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow, monks, a sitting mat and a small sitting mat.
Now at that time, sick monks had need of medicinal decoctions.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow, monks, astringent medicinal decoctions:
neem decoction, *kuṭaja* decoction, *paṭola* decoction, *phaggava* decoction, *nattamālaka* decoction,
or whatever other astringent medicinal decoctions there may be that do not serve as food for the purpose of eating.”
They do not dedicate edible food for the purpose of edible food, [but rather] so that,
having received them, they may keep them for as long as life lasts and consume them when there is a suitable occasion.
“There is an offense of wrong-doing for one who consumes it when there is no requisite cause.
Now at that time, sick monks had need of medicines prepared from leaves.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, leaf medicines:
neem leaves, kuṭaja leaves, bitter gourd leaves, sulasī leaves, cotton-tree leaves,
or whatever other leaf medicines there may be that do not serve as a staple food for the purpose of a staple food, nor serve as a non-staple food for the purpose of a non-staple food.”
... At that time, the sick monks had need of medicinal fruits.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow, monks, medicinal fruits:
*bilanga*, long pepper, black pepper, yellow myrobalan, beleric myrobalan, emblic myrobalan, *goṭṭhaphala*,
or whatever other medicinal fruits there may be that do not function as solid food for the purpose of solid food.”
They did not distribute edible food for the purpose of edible food … [and so on] … Now at that time, sick bhikkhus had need of medicinal ghee.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“I allow you, monks, resin medicines:

asafoetida, asafoetida-resin, asafoetida-powder, buttermilk, buttermilk-skin, buttermilk-leaf, *sajjulasa*, or whatever other resin medicines there may be that do not serve the purpose of solid food as solid food.”
... At that time, the sick monks had need of salt medicines.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow medicinal salts:

sea salt, black salt, rock salt, biḷāla salt, sochal salt, and whatever other medicinal salts there may be that do not serve the purpose of fresh food when taken as fresh food, nor serve the purpose of cooked food when taken as cooked food.
Having accepted these, one may keep them for as long as life lasts.”
"One may consume it when there is a requisite condition;
for one who consumes it when there is no requisite condition, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
Now at that time, Venerable Belaṭṭhasīsa, the preceptor of Venerable Ānanda, was suffering from a severe skin disease.
His robes would stick to his body because of the synovial fluid; the monks would repeatedly moisten them with water and pull them off.
While wandering about the lodgings, the Blessed One saw those monks repeatedly moistening the robes with water and pulling them off.
Having seen this, he approached those monks, and having approached, he said this to them:
“Monks, what is this monk’s ailment?
“Venerable sir, this venerable one has the ailment of severe itch; his robes stick to his body because of the discharge. We moisten them again and again with water and pull them off.
Then the Blessed One, on this occasion and in this connection, having given a Dhamma talk, addressed the monks:
“I allow, monks, medicinal powders for one who has an affliction such as an itch, a boil, a discharge, or severe scabies, or whose body has a foul odor.
I allow, monks, for one who is not ill, fermented soil, clay, and dye-liquor.
I allow, monks, a mortar and pestle.”
Now at that time, the sick monks had need of medicinal powders that had been stirred into a liquid.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
"I allow you, monks, a powder-stirring ladle," he said.
“There is a purpose for what is gentle.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow a cloth-strainer,” he said.
Now at that time, a certain monk was afflicted by a non-human illness.
Although his teachers and preceptors attended to him, they were unable to restore him to health.
He went to a pigsty and ate raw meat and drank raw blood.
His affliction caused by non-human beings subsided.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“Monks, I allow raw meat and raw blood in the case of an affliction caused by non-human beings.”
Now at that time, a certain monk was afflicted with an eye disease.
The monks, supporting him, were carrying him out even for the sake of excrement and urine.
The Blessed One, while wandering on a tour of the lodgings, saw those monks supporting that monk.
Seeing them voiding excrement and urine, he approached those bhikkhus and, having approached,
said to them: "Bhikkhus,
what is this illness of this bhikkhu?"
“Venerable sir, this venerable one has an affliction of eye disease.
Having taken him under our care, we have been assisting him even in the evacuation of excrement and urine.
Then the Blessed One, on that occasion and in that connection, having given a discourse on the Dhamma, addressed the bhikkhus:
“I allow, monks, collyrium:
black collyrium, resinous collyrium, eye-salve, red chalk, and stone-powder.
There was a need for the grinding of the collyrium.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow, monks, sandalwood, tagara, kāḷānusāriya, tālīsa, and bhaddamuttaka.
Now at that time, the monks were storing powdered ointments in both bowls and saucers.
They were being strewn with grass-dust and even with soil.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow an ointment-box,” he said.
Now at that time, the group of six monks carried various kinds of ointment boxes—
some made of gold, some made of silver.
People complained, grumbled, and became indignant, saying:
“It is just like householders who enjoy sensual pleasures.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, a luxurious ointment box should not be carried.”
Whoever should wear one, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
“I allow you, monks, [an ointment box] made of bone, made of ivory, made of horn, made of reed, made of bamboo, made of wood, made of lac, made of fruit, made of metal, or made of conch-shell.
Now at that time, ointment boxes were left open and were being sprinkled with grass-dust and soil.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow a lid,” he said.
The lid fell off.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow you to bind it with a thread and then attach it to a cosmetic box.
The cosmetic box broke.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow you to sew with thread,” he said.
Now at that time, the monks applied ointment with their fingers, and their eyes became painful.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, an ointment-stick,” he said.
Now at that time, the group of six monks were carrying various kinds of high-quality ointment-sticks.
It was made of gold and silver.
People complained, grumbled, and became indignant, saying,
"This is just like householders who indulge in sensual pleasures."
They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“Monks, various kinds of eye-salve sticks should not be kept.
Whoever should keep them, there is an offense of wrong-doing.”
“I allow, monks, [an ointment stick] made of bone... up to ... made of conch-shell.
Now at that time, the ointment sticks, having fallen on the ground, became rough.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow, monks, a case for the ointment stick.
Now at that time, the monks were carrying both the ointment box and the ointment stick in their hands.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow, monks, a case for ointment,” [the Blessed One said].
There was no shoulder-strap.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow, monks, a shoulder-strap and a binding cord.
Now at that time, Venerable Pilindavaccha suffered from a fever in his head.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow, monks, oil on the head.
It was not pleasing.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow, monks, the administration of medicine through the nose.
The medicine flowed out of the nose.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow, monks, a nose-tube.
Now at that time, the group-of-six monks used various kinds of nose-tubes—
some made of gold, some made of silver.
People criticized, complained, and grumbled, saying,
“They are just like householders who indulge in sensual pleasures.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, a luxurious nose-treatment instrument should not be used.
Whoever should use one, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Monks, I allow [an instrument] made of bone …” [and so forth].
"Made of conch-shell.
They were pouring it into the nose unevenly.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow, monks, a twin nose-cleansing stick.
It was not satisfactory.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, to drink smoke.
They lit that very wick and drank it; their throats burned.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow, monks, a smoking pipe.
Now at that time, the group-of-six monks used various kinds of smoking pipes,
including those made of gold and silver.
People criticized, grumbled, and complained, saying,
“They are just like householders who indulge in sensual pleasures.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, smoke-tubes of various kinds should not be used.
Whoever should use one, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Monks, I allow [tubes] made of bone …pe… made of conch-shell.”
Now at that time, the smoke-pipes were left open, and insects entered them.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow a cover,” he said.
Now at that time, the monks were carrying the smoking tubes with their hands.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow a case for the smoking tube.”
They struck them on one side.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow a double-sided wooden mallet.”
There was no shoulder strap.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow a shoulder strap made of binding thread,” he said.
Now at that time, Venerable Pilindavaccha suffered from a wind ailment.
The physicians said,
"Oil must be cooked."
They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“Monks, I allow oil-medicines.
Now, in that oil-medicine, fermented liquor was to be added.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow you to add intoxicating liquor to oil preparations,” he said.
Now at that time, the group of six monks cooked oils into which too much intoxicating liquor had been added; having drunk them, they became intoxicated.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“Monks, oil that has been excessively saturated with alcohol must not be drunk.
Whoever should drink it is to be dealt with according to the rule.”
“I allow you, monks, to drink oil that has been cooked with liquor in such a way that neither the color, nor the smell, nor the taste of the liquor is discernible.
Now at that time, much oil that had been cooked with too much added liquor was ready for the monks. Then it occurred to the monks:
“How now should one proceed regarding oil that has been cooked with too much added liquor?”
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow you to consecrate ointment,” he said.
Now at that time, a large amount of oil had been prepared for the Venerable Pilindavaccha, but no oil vessel was available.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow three kinds of vessels:
a metal vessel, a wooden vessel, and a fruit vessel.”
Now at that time, Venerable Pilindavaccha had a rheumatic condition.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow the application of sweating therapy,” he said.
He became difficult to endure.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow the use of a mixture for soothing,” [the Blessed One said].
He became difficult to endure.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow a great poultice,” he said.
He was difficult to appease.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow you broken rice water,” he said.
He was difficult to endure.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow a water-cistern,” he said.
Now at that time, Venerable Pilindavaccha had a fever.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
"I allow you, monks, to let blood," [the Blessed One said].
He became difficult to treat.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow you, having bled [the wound], to apply a horn [ointment].”
Now at that time, the venerable Pilindavaccha’s feet were cracked.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow foot ointment.”
He became difficult to endure.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“Monks, I allow you to prepare a foot-salve.”
Now at that time, a certain monk suffered from an abscess.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, surgical treatment,” he said.
There was need for decoction water.
They informed the Blessed One of this matter.
“Monks, I allow decoction water,” he said.
There was need for sesame paste.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“Monks, I allow sesame paste.”
There was need for a bowl.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, a bowl,” he said.
There was need for a bandage-cloth for wounds.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, a bandage-cloth for wounds,” he said.
The wound itched.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow you to sprinkle it with mustard-powder,” he said.
The wound festered.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow you to apply smoke [as a treatment],” he said.
The meat grew back.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow you to cut it with salt crystals,” he said.
"A wound does not heal.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
"Monks, I allow wound-oil," he said.
The oil leaked away.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow a cotton wick for all treatments of wounds.”
Now at that time, a certain bhikkhu had been bitten by a snake.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
"I allow you, bhikkhus, to give four kinds of formidable things: [the flesh of] a dog, a snake, a monkey, and a human."
“Feces, urine, ash, and clay.
Then it occurred to the monks:
“Are these not to be accepted, or should they be accepted?”
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow you, when there is a kappiyakāraka (one who makes things allowable), to have it accepted by him; when there is no kappiyakāraka, to take it up yourself and consume it.
Now at that time, a certain monk had drunk poison.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow you to give dung to drink,” he said.
Then it occurred to the monks:
“Is it indeed unaccepted, or should it be accepted?
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, that when one accepts while performing [an action], that itself constitutes acceptance; it need not be accepted again.”
Now at that time, a certain monk suffered from a disease called *gharadinnaka*.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow you to give him a cold gruel to drink,” he said.
Now at that time, a certain monk was suffering from a chronic ailment.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow you to give him a decoction of food to drink.”
Now at that time, a certain monk was afflicted with jaundice.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow you to give him to drink *muttaharītaka* (myrobalan processed with urine),” [the Blessed One said].
Now at that time, a certain monk was afflicted with the disease of putrefaction.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow you to apply fragrant ointments,” he said.
Now at that time, a certain monk had a body full of humors.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow you to drink a purgative,” he said.
There was need for bear broth.
They informed the Blessed One of this matter.
“Monks, I allow bear broth,” he said.
There was need for uncooked gruel.
They informed the Blessed One of this matter.
“I allow you, monks, uncooked gruel,” he said.
“There is need for *kaṭākaṭa*.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow *kaṭākaṭa*,” he said.
“There is a need for a covering cloth.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, a covering cloth,” he said.
3. The Story of Pilindavaccha Now at that time, the Venerable Pilindavaccha was having a mountain slope cleared at Rājagaha, desiring to build a cave-dwelling.
Then King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha approached the Venerable Pilindavaccha; having approached, he paid homage to the Venerable Pilindavaccha and sat down to one side.
As he was sitting to one side, King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha said to the Venerable Pilindavaccha, "Venerable sir, what is the Elder having done?
"Great king, I am having a mountain slope cleared; I wish to have a cave constructed."
“Venerable sir, would it be beneficial for the noble one to have an attendant?
“Great king, an attendant has not been permitted by the Blessed One.
“In that case, venerable sir, please inquire of the Blessed One and let me know.”
“Yes, Great King,” the Venerable Pilindavaccha replied to Seniya Bimbisāra, the King of Magadha.
Then the Venerable Pilindavaccha instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha with a discourse on the Dhamma.
Then King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha, [having been] by the Venerable Pilindavaccha... with a discourse on the Dhamma...
Having been instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened, he rose from his seat, paid homage to the Venerable Pilindavaccha,
circumambulated him with his right side toward him, and departed.
Then the Venerable Pilindavaccha sent a messenger to the Blessed One, saying:
“Venerable sir, King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha wishes to give an attendant to the monastery.
How, venerable sir, should I proceed?
Then, on this occasion and in this context, the Blessed One gave a discourse on the Dhamma and addressed the bhikkhus:
“I allow you, monks, a monastery attendant.
A second time, King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha approached the Venerable Pilindavaccha; having approached, he paid homage to the Venerable Pilindavaccha and sat down to one side.
As he was sitting there, King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha said this to the Venerable Pilindavaccha:
“Venerable sir, has the Blessed One permitted a monastery attendant?
“Yes, great king.
“In that case, venerable sir, I shall give a monastery attendant to the noble one.”

Then King Seniya Bimbisāra of Māgadha, having agreed to provide a monastery attendant for the venerable Pilindavaccha, forgot about it; after a long time he regained his memory and addressed a certain high minister who was in charge of all affairs:
“My good man, did I agree to give a monastery attendant to the noble one?
“I did not, Your Majesty, give a monastery attendant to the noble one.”
“How long, my good man, has it been since then?
Then that chief minister, having counted the nights, said this to King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha:
“Five hundred nights, Your Majesty.”
“In that case, my good man, give five hundred monastery attendants to the noble one.

“Very well, Your Majesty,” the high minister replied to King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha, and he gave five hundred monastery attendants to the Venerable Pilindavaccha; a separate village was established for them.
They called it “Ārāmikagāmaka,” and they also called it “Pilindagāmaka.
Now at that time, the Venerable Pilindavaccha was visiting the families in that village.
Then, in the morning, the Venerable Pilindavaccha dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Pilindagāma for alms.
Now at that time, there was a festival in that village.
The children were playing, adorned with ornaments and garlands.

Then the Venerable Pilindavaccha, while wandering for alms from house to house in Pilindagāma, approached the residence of a certain monastery attendant; having arrived, he sat down on the seat prepared for him.
Now at that time, the daughter of that female monastery attendant, seeing other children adorned and garlanded, began to weep, saying, "Give me a garland! Give me an ornament!
Then the Venerable Pilindavaccha said this to the female monastery attendant:
“Why is this girl crying?
“Venerable sir, having seen other girls adorned and garlanded, this girl cries out:
‘Give me a garland! Give me an ornament!’”
“Where would we, who are so unfortunate, have garlands? Where would we have ornaments?
Then the Venerable Pilindavaccha took a bundle of grass and said to that female monastery attendant, “Well now, tie this bundle of grass around the head of that girl.”
Then that park-keeper took that bundle of grass and tied it upon the head of that girl.
It became a golden garland—beautiful, lovely to behold, and inspiring;
there was no such golden garland even in the king’s own inner apartments.
People reported to King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha:
"In the house of such-and-such a monastery attendant, Your Majesty, there is a golden garland that is beautiful, lovely to behold, and inspiring;
even in the royal palace, Your Majesty, there is no golden garland like it."
"How could that wretched man have it?
Without a doubt, it was brought by theft.
Then King Seniya Bimbisāra of Māgadha had that family of monastery attendants bound.
A second time, the Venerable Pilindavaccha, having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, entered Pilindagāma for alms.

While walking for alms from house to house in Pilindagāma, he approached the residence of that monastery attendant; having approached, he asked the neighbors, "Where has this family of the monastery attendant gone?"
“Venerable sir, it was for the sake of that golden garland that the king had me imprisoned.
Then the Venerable Pilindavaccha went to the residence of Seniya Bimbisāra, the King of Magadha; having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat.
Then King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha approached the Venerable Pilindavaccha, and having approached and paid homage to the Venerable Pilindavaccha, he sat down to one side.

“Great King, why has the family of the monastery attendant been imprisoned?

Whatever he receives, he distributes to the assembly.
His assembly is characterized by abundance;
whatever he receives, he collects and stores it, filling even jars and pots.
Having filled even the water-strainers and bags, he hung them from the windows;
they remained there, dangling and swaying.
The monasteries were also strewn and scattered all over with rats.

"How can these monks consent to such abundance?

Then the Blessed One, wandering by stages on his tour, arrived at Rājagaha. There, the Blessed One stayed near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, at the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.

Now at that time, the monks—

They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, to cook it again.
Now at that time, Rājagaha was suffering from a famine.
People brought salt, oil, rice, and hard foods to the monastery.
The monks had them stored outside;
ants ate them, and thieves also carried them off.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow you to keep it indoors,” [the Blessed One said].
Having kept it indoors, they cooked it outdoors.
The tamers surrounded them.
The monks ate without confidence.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow you to cook inside [the monastery].”
During a time of famine, the kitchen attendants took more for themselves and gave less to the monks.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow you to cook for yourselves.”
“I allow you, monks, what has been stored indoors, cooked indoors, and cooked by oneself.
Now at that time, a number of monks who had completed the rains retreat in Kāsī were traveling toward Rājagaha.
On the way to see the Blessed One, they were unable to obtain as much as they needed for their full satisfaction of either coarse or refined food;
yet there was an abundance of fruit to eat.

Then those monks, appearing weary, approached Rājagaha, the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place, where the Blessed One was; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side.
Now it is the custom for the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, to exchange greetings with visiting monks.
Then the Blessed One said this to those bhikkhus:
“I hope, bhikkhus, that you are bearing up, I hope you are getting by,
and I hope you have come along the road without too much fatigue?”
“And from where have you come, monks?
“It is bearable, Blessed One; it is livable, Blessed One.

Here, Bhante, having spent the rains retreat among the Kāsīs, we were coming to Rājagaha to see the Blessed One, but along the way we did not obtain sufficient quantities of either coarse or refined food to our heart’s content.”
"There was much fruit and fresh food,
but there was no one to prepare what is allowable;
therefore, we have come along this road looking quite exhausted."
Then the Blessed One, having given a discourse on the Dhamma on this occasion and in this context, addressed the bhikkhus:

“I allow you, bhikkhus, wherever one sees fresh fruit and there is no attendant for what is allowable, to take it oneself, carry it away, and upon seeing an attendant for what is allowable, set it down on the ground, have it formally accepted, and then consume it.
I allow you, bhikkhus, to accept what has been picked up.”
Now at that time, fresh sesame seeds and fresh honey had come into the possession of a certain brahmin.
Then it occurred to that brahmin:
"What if I were to give these fresh sesame seeds and fresh honey to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha?"
Then that brahmin approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, he stood to one side.
Standing to one side, that brahmin said this to the Blessed One:
“May the venerable Gotama accept my meal for tomorrow, together with the community of bhikkhus.”
The Blessed One consented by remaining silent.
Then that brahmin, understanding the Blessed One’s consent, departed.
When that night had passed, the brahmin had various kinds of fine food, both hard and soft, prepared and had the time announced to the Blessed One: [“It is time, sir; the meal is ready”].
“It is time, Master Gotama; the meal is ready.

Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, went to the residence of that brahmin. Having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat together with the community of monks.

Then that brahmin, with his own hands, served and satisfied the community of monks headed by the Buddha with excellent hard and soft foods. When the Blessed One had finished eating and had withdrawn his hand from the bowl, the brahmin sat down to one side.
When that brahmin was seated to one side, the Blessed One instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened him with a discourse on the Dhamma; then, rising from his seat, he departed.
Not long after the Blessed One had left, it occurred to that brahmin:
"For whose sake did I invite the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha, thinking, 'I will give fresh sesame seeds and fresh honey'? I have forgotten to give them."
“What if I were to have fresh sesame seeds and fresh honey brought to the monastery in jars and pots?
Then that brahmin had fresh sesame seeds and fresh honey brought to the monastery in jars and pots, and he approached the Blessed One; having approached, he stood to one side.
Standing to one side, that brahmin said this to the Blessed One:
“Master Gotama, those for whose sake I invited the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha, thinking, ‘I will give fresh sesame seeds and fresh honey,’ I have forgotten to give them.
May Master Gotama accept from me the fresh sesame seeds and the fresh honey.
“In that case, brahmin, give them to the bhikkhus.”
Now at that time, during a famine, the monks were offering invitations even for very small amounts;
they would also refuse after due consideration, and the entire Saṅgha had already been invited. Being afraid of wrongdoing, the monks did not accept.

“Having shown it to the Venerable Upananda, it should be given to the Saṅgha.

“Venerable sir, where is the noble Upananda?
“Friend, that venerable Upananda, the son of the Sakyans, has entered the village for alms.
“Venerable sir, having shown this fresh food to the noble Upananda, it should be given to the Saṅgha.”

“In that case, monks, accept it and set it aside until Upananda arrives.

“I allow you, monks, to consume what has been received before the meal by one who has already eaten and finished his meal, provided it is not leftover.
Then the Blessed One, having stayed at Rājagaha for as long as he pleased, set out on a wandering tour toward Sāvatthī.

At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna approached the Venerable Sāriputta and, having approached him, said this to the Venerable Sāriputta:
“Friend Sāriputta, what used to relieve your bodily burning ailment in the past?
“By means of lotus roots and stalks, friend.

Just as one might stretch out an arm, or bend back an arm that has been stretched out, even so, having vanished from Jeta’s Grove, he reappeared on the bank of the Mandākinī lotus pond.

After the Venerable Sāriputta had eaten the lotus roots and stalks, his bodily ailment of fever subsided.

Now at that time, during a period of famine, the monks were offering invitations even for very small amounts; they would refuse after due reflection, and the entire Saṅgha had already been invited.
Being afraid of wrongdoing, the monks did not accept.
[The Buddha said: "Accept, monks, and consume."
“I allow you, monks, to consume forest-grown or lotus-root grown food that has not been left over, provided one has finished eating and has refused further offerings.

The monks, being afraid of wrongdoing, did not consume the fruit.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow you to consume fruit that is seedless, from which seeds have been removed, and which has not been prepared.

Then the Blessed One, having stayed at Sāvatthī for as long as he pleased, set out on a wandering tour toward Rājagaha.
Traveling by stages on his tour, he arrived at Rājagaha.
There, the Blessed One stayed at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, at the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Now at that time, a certain monk was afflicted with a hemorrhoid.
A physician of the Ākāsagotta clan was performing surgery on him.
Then the Blessed One, while wandering on a tour of the lodgings, approached the dwelling of that monk.
The physician Ākāsagotta saw the Blessed One coming from afar; having seen him, he said this to the Blessed One:
“May Master Gotama come; let him look at the anus of this bhikkhu, just like the mouth of a lizard.

“‘This foolish man is mocking me’”— thinking thus,
he turned back from that very place, and having convened the community of monks on this occasion and for this purpose,
he questioned the monks: “Is there, monks, a sick monk in such-and-such a monastery?”
“There is, Blessed One.
“What is that bhikkhu’s affliction, monks?
“Venerable sir, that venerable one has hemorrhoids; a physician named Ākāsagotta is performing surgery on him.”
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked him:
“Monks, it is unseemly for that misguided man, it is unbecoming, improper, unworthy of a recluse, unallowable, and not to be done.

“Monks, in a cramped place, the skin is delicate, the wound is difficult to treat, and the knife is hard to manage.

“Bhikkhus, surgical treatment should not be performed on a constricted area.

"How can the group-of-six monks have a vaginal douche performed?

“Is it true, monks, that the group-of-six monks have had a vaginal douche performed?
“It is true, Blessed One.
… Having rebuked them and given a discourse on the Dhamma, he addressed the monks:
“Monks, surgical treatment or cauterization should not be performed within two finger-breadths of a constricted area.
Whoever should have it performed incurs a *thullaccaya* offense. 9.
Discussion on the Prohibition of Human Flesh.

"Who, venerable sirs, is ill? What should be brought for whom?"

Then that bhikkhu said this to the female lay follower Suppiyā:
“Sister, I have drunk a purgative.”
“I have need of something to cover myself with.

then, having gone home, he commanded his pupil:

“There is no meat available, noble lady.

Then the male lay follower Suppiya thought:
“How wonderful, indeed! How marvelous, indeed!”
“Since Suppiyā is so full of faith and confidence that she has even given away her own flesh, what else could there be that she would not give?

As Suppiya the lay follower was sitting to one side, he said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, may the Blessed One accept tomorrow’s meal from me, together with the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.

“Monks, human flesh must not be consumed.

“Whoever should consume it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.

whether it be an assembly of kshatriyas, an assembly of brahmins, an assembly of householders, or an assembly of ascetics—

This is the third benefit for one who is virtuous through the perfection of virtue.
Furthermore, householders, one who is virtuous and perfected in virtue dies unconfused.
This is the fourth benefit for one who is virtuous through the perfection of virtue.
Furthermore, householders, one who is virtuous and perfected in virtue, with the breakup of the body after death, is reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world.
This is the fifth benefit for one who is virtuous through the perfection of virtue.
“Householders, these are the five benefits for one who is virtuous and possesses the perfection of virtue.
Then the Blessed One, having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened the lay followers of Pāṭaligāma with a discourse on the Dharma for much of the night, dismissed them, saying:
“The night has passed, householders.”
"Now, you may consider it time to depart.

"Very well, Bhante," the lay followers of Pāṭaligāma replied to the Blessed One. Having risen from their seats, they paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him with their right side toward him, and departed.
Then, not long after the lay followers of Pāṭaligāma had left, the Blessed One entered an empty dwelling.
15. The Account of Sunidha and Vassakāra Now at that time, Sunidha and Vassakāra, the chief ministers of Magadha, were building a city at Pāṭaligāma as a bulwark against the Vajjis.
Then, having risen at the end of the night, the Blessed One, with the purified divine eye surpassing that of humans, saw many deities taking possession of sites in Pāṭaligāma.
In whatever place powerful deities take possession of sites, the minds of powerful kings and royal ministers incline toward building residences there.
In whatever place deities of middling power take possession of sites, the minds of middling kings and royal ministers incline toward building residences there.
In whatever place low-ranking deities take possession of sites, the minds of low-ranking kings and royal ministers incline toward building residences there.
Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
“Ānanda, who is it that is building a city at Pāṭaligāma?
“Venerable sir, Sunidha and Vassakāra, the chief ministers of Magadha, are building a city at Pāṭaligāma to ward off the Vajjis.”
“Ānanda, just as if one were consulting with the gods of the Thirty-three,
even so, Ānanda, Sunidha and Vassakāra, the chief ministers of Magadha, are building a city at Pāṭaligāma to ward off the Vajjis.
Here, Ānanda, rising at the time of dawn during the night, I saw with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, many deities taking possession of sites in Pāṭaligāma.”
In whatever place powerful deities take possession of sites, the minds of powerful kings and royal ministers incline toward building dwellings there.
In whatever place middling deities take possession of sites, the minds of middling kings and royal ministers incline toward building dwellings there.
In whatever place inferior deities take possession of sites, the minds of inferior kings and royal ministers incline toward building dwellings there.
“Ānanda, as far as the noble realm extends, as far as the marketplace extends, this city of Pāṭaliputta, a great port, will be the foremost city.
But for Pāṭaliputta, Ānanda, there will be three dangers:
from fire, from water, or from internal dissension.”

Then Sunidha and Vassakāra, the chief ministers of Magadha, approached the Blessed One. Having approached, they exchanged greetings with the Blessed One; and when they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, they stood to one side.
Standing to one side, Sunidha and Vassakāra, the chief ministers of Magadha, said this to the Blessed One:
“May the venerable Gotama accept today’s meal from us, together with the community of monks.”
The Blessed One consented by remaining silent.
Then Sunidha and Vassakāra, the chief ministers of Magadha, understanding the Blessed One’s consent, departed.

Thereupon, Sunidha and Vassakāra, the chief ministers of Magadha, having had choice food, both hard and soft, prepared, had the time announced to the Blessed One: “It is time, Master Gotama; the meal is ready.”
Then, in the morning, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and robe, and went to the dining hall of Sunidha and Vassakāra,
the chief ministers of Magadha; having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat together with the community of monks.
Then Sunidha and Vassakāra, the chief ministers of Magadha, having personally served and satisfied the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha with excellent hard and soft foods,
sat down to one side when the Blessed One had finished his meal and had withdrawn his hand from the bowl.
When Sunīdha and Vassakāra, the two chief ministers of Magadha, were seated to one side, the Blessed One expressed his appreciation with these verses:
“In whatever place a person of wise nature makes his dwelling, [there he finds success].”
Having fed here those who are virtuous,
self-restrained, and leading the holy life,
whatever deities were present there—
One should designate them as the recipients of offerings;
when they are honored, they honor him in return, and when they are respected, they show respect to him.
Then the deities show him compassion,
just as a mother does for her own biological son;
a person who is thus favored by the deities—
“...one always sees auspicious things.
Then the Blessed One, having expressed his appreciation to Sunidha and Vassakāra, the chief ministers of Magadha, with these verses, rose from his seat and departed.
At that time, Sunidha and Vassakāra, the chief ministers of Magadha, followed closely behind the Blessed One.
“Whatever gate the ascetic Gotama shall depart from today shall be known as ‘Gotama’s Gate’;
whatever ford he shall cross the river Gaṅgā at shall be known as ‘Gotama’s Ford.
Then, the gate through which the Blessed One departed became known as Gotama’s Gate.
Then the Blessed One approached the river Gaṅgā.
Now at that time the river Gaṅgā was full, level with its banks, so that a crow could drink from it.
Some people were searching for boats, others were searching for rafts, and others were binding together floats, desiring to go from this shore to the far shore.
The Blessed One saw those people— some seeking a boat, some seeking a raft, and others binding a raft,
desiring to go from this shore to the further shore— and having seen them,
just as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm or draw in his extended arm, even so did he vanish from the near bank of the river Ganges.
Having vanished, he reappeared on the opposite shore together with the community of monks.
Then the Blessed One, having understood this matter, on that occasion uttered this inspired exclamation:
“Those who cross the ocean-like flood, the lake...”
Having built a bridge and left behind the marshes,
people indeed construct a raft;
but it is the wise who have already crossed over.
16. The Discourse on the Truth at Koṭigāma.
Then the Blessed One went to Koṭigāma.
There, indeed, the Blessed One stayed at Koṭigāma.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, it is through not awakening to and not penetrating four noble truths that we have wandered and transmigrated for such a long time, both I and you. Which four?
“Bhikkhus, it is through not awakening to and not penetrating the noble truth of suffering that we have wandered and transmigrated for so long a time—
both I and you. It is through not awakening to and not penetrating the noble truth of the origin of suffering … [and] the noble truth of the cessation of suffering …”
"Because of the non-awakening and non-penetration of the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering, this long journey has been traversed and wandered through by both you and me.
But now, monks, that noble truth of suffering has been awakened to and penetrated; the noble truth of the origin of suffering has been awakened to and penetrated;
the noble truth of the cessation of suffering has been awakened to and penetrated; [and] the way leading to the cessation of suffering..."

The noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering has been awakened to and penetrated; the craving for existence has been severed, the conduit to existence has been destroyed, and there is now no further becoming.
Of the four noble truths—
Through not seeing things as they truly are,
one has wandered for a long time through this or that very birth.
These views have been seen through,
the conduit to existence has been uprooted;
the root of suffering is severed.
“There is now no further becoming.
17. The Story of Ambapālī:
The courtesan Ambapālī heard this.
“Indeed, the Blessed One has arrived at Koṭigāma.
Then Ambapālī the courtesan had fine carriages harnessed, mounted a fine carriage herself, and set out from Vesālī with the fine carriages to see the Blessed One.

She went by carriage as far as the ground would allow for a vehicle, then alighted from the carriage and approached the Blessed One on foot. Having approached, she paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
As Ambapālī the courtesan sat to one side, the Blessed One instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened her with a discourse on the Dhamma.
Then Ambapālī the courtesan, having been instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened by the Blessed One’s discourse on the Dhamma, said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, may the Blessed One accept tomorrow’s meal from me, together with the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.”
The Blessed One consented by remaining silent.
Then Ambapālī the courtesan, understanding the Blessed One’s consent, rose from her seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him to her right, departed.
18. The Account of the Licchavis.
The Licchavis of Vesālī heard:
“The Blessed One, it is said, has arrived at Koṭigāma.
Then the Licchavis of Vesālī had their fine carriages harnessed; mounting each of their fine carriages, they set out from Vesālī in their fine carriages to see the Blessed One.
Some Licchavis were blue—blue in color, wearing blue garments, and adorned with blue ornaments;
some Licchavis were yellow—yellow in color, wearing yellow garments, and adorned with yellow ornaments; some Licchavis were red—red in color, wearing red garments, and adorned with red ornaments;
and some Licchavis were white—white in color, wearing white garments, and adorned with white ornaments.

Then Ambapālī the courtesan drove her carriage so that its pole was against their pole, its yoke against their yoke, its wheel against their wheel, and its axle against their axle, right up against those young Licchavis.
Then those Licchavis said this to Ambapālī the courtesan:

“For what reason, dear Ambapālī, do you drive your carriage so that its pole is against their pole, its yoke against their yoke, its wheel against their wheel, and its axle against their axle, right up against those young Licchavis?”
“However, noble sirs, I have invited the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, headed by the Buddha, for tomorrow’s meal.
“Give this meal to us, Ambapālī, for a hundred thousand pieces of gold!
“Even if you were to give me the entire city of Vesālī along with its territory, noble sirs, I would still not give up that meal.”
Then those Licchavis snapped their fingers, saying, "We have indeed been defeated by Ambakā! We have indeed been conquered by Ambakā!
Then those Licchavis approached the Blessed One.
The Blessed One saw those Licchavis coming from afar, and having seen them, he addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, those bhikkhus who have never before seen the gods of the Thirty-three, look upon this assembly of Licchavis;
gaze upon this assembly of Licchavis.”
“Bhikkhus, compare the assembly of the Licchavis to the assembly of the Thirty-three.
Then those Licchavis went by vehicle as far as the ground would allow for a vehicle; having alighted from their vehicles, they approached the Blessed One on foot.
Having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
As those Licchavis were sitting to one side, the Blessed One instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened them with a discourse on the Dhamma.
Then, having been instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened by the Blessed One’s discourse on the Dhamma, those Licchavis said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, may the Blessed One accept our meal tomorrow, together with the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.”
“I have already accepted Ambapālī the courtesan’s meal for tomorrow, Licchavis,” he said.
Then those Licchavis snapped their fingers, saying, “We have been defeated by Ambakā!
We have been utterly vanquished by Ambakā!”
Then those Licchavis, having rejoiced and delighted in the Blessed One’s words, rose from their seats, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him to their right, departed.
Then the Blessed One, having stayed at Koṭigāma for as long as he pleased, went to Nādika.
There, the Blessed One stayed at Nādika in the Brick House.

Then, at the end of that night, the courtesan Ambapālī had various kinds of excellent hard and soft food prepared in her own park and had the time announced to the Blessed One: “It is time, venerable sir; the meal is ready.

Then, in the morning, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and robe, and went to where the courtesan Ambapālī’s dining hall was; having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat together with the community of monks.
Then the courtesan Ambapālī, having personally satisfied and served the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha with excellent hard and soft foods,
sat down to one side when the Blessed One had finished his meal and had withdrawn his hand from the bowl.
Sitting there to one side, the courtesan Ambapālī addressed the Blessed One thus:
“Venerable sir, I give this mango grove to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha.
The Blessed One accepted the monastery.
Then the Blessed One, having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened Ambapālī the courtesan with a Dhamma talk, rose from his seat and went toward the Great Forest.
There the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī in the Great Wood, in the Gabled Hall.
The third section on the Licchavis is finished.
19. The Account of General Sīha.
Now at that time, many well-known Licchavis were seated together and assembled in the assembly hall,
praising the Buddha in many ways, praising the Dhamma in many ways, and praising the Saṅgha in many ways.
At that time, Sīha the general, a disciple of the Nigaṇṭhas, was sitting in that assembly.
Then it occurred to Sīha the general:
"Without doubt, that Blessed One must be an Arahant, a perfectly awakened Buddha;
for these well-known Licchavis, having sat down and assembled in the assembly hall, have praised the Buddha in many ways."
“They speak in praise of the Dhamma; they speak in praise of the Saṅgha.
What if I were to approach that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One, in order to see him?
Then the general Sīha approached the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta; having approached, he said this to the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta:
“I wish, venerable sir, to go and see the ascetic Gotama.
“But why, Sīha, being yourself a proponent of action, would you go to see the ascetic Gotama, who is a proponent of non-action?

Then Sīha the general’s intention to go and see the Blessed One subsided.

“Without a doubt, that Blessed One must be an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha;
for these well-known Licchavis, having sat down and assembled in the council hall, are praising the Buddha in many ways,
praising the Dharma, and praising the Saṅgha.”
"What if I were now to approach that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, for the purpose of seeing him?
For a second time, Sīha the general approached the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta; having approached, he said this to the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta:
"Venerable sir, I wish to approach the ascetic Gotama for the purpose of seeing him."
“But why, Sīha, being yourself a proponent of action, would you go to see the ascetic Gotama, a proponent of non-action?
For the ascetic Gotama, Sīha, is a proponent of non-action; he teaches a doctrine of non-action and trains his disciples therein.
A second time, the general Sīha’s intention to go and see the Blessed One subsided.
A third time, the well-known Licchavis, having assembled and gathered together in the assembly hall, spoke in many ways in praise of the Buddha, in praise of the Dhamma, and in praise of the Saṅgha.
A third time, it occurred to Sīha the general:
"Without doubt, that Blessed One must be an Arhat, a perfectly enlightened Buddha; for these well-known [Licchavis]..."
The well-known Licchavis, seated together and assembled in the assembly hall, were praising the Buddha in many ways,
praising the Dhamma, and praising the Saṅgha.
"What can these Nigaṇṭhas do to me, whether they have been consulted or not?"
"What if I were to go to see that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, without even taking leave of the Nigaṇṭhas?
Then General Sīha set out from Vesālī during the day with five hundred chariots to see the Blessed One.

As far as the ground was passable for a vehicle, he went by vehicle; then, alighting from the vehicle, he approached the Blessed One on foot. Having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, the general Sīha said this to the Blessed One:
“I have heard this, Bhante: ‘The ascetic Gotama is a proponent of non-action; he teaches a doctrine of non-action, and by that he trains his disciples.
Those who speak thus, Bhante, say: ‘The ascetic Gotama is a proponent of non-action; he teaches a doctrine of non-action, and by that he trains his disciples.’”

“Venerable sir, do they speak in accordance with what was said by the Blessed One? Do they not misrepresent the Blessed One with what is false? Do they explain the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma? And does no legitimate criticism or reproach arise against them from a fellow follower of the Dhamma?
For we do not wish to misrepresent the Blessed One, venerable sir.
“There is a way, Sīha, by which one speaking rightly might say of me: ‘The recluse Gotama is one who eats whatever is given to him.’”
“The ascetic Gotama is a proponent of non-action; he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of non-action, and by that he trains his disciples.
“There is, Sīha, a way in which one speaking rightly could say of me:
‘The ascetic Gotama is a proponent of action; he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of action, and by that he trains his disciples.’”
"There is, Sīha, a way in which one speaking rightly might say of me:
'The ascetic Gotama is an annihilationist; he teaches a doctrine for the sake of annihilation, and by that he trains his disciples.
There is, Sīha, a way in which one speaking rightly might say of me:"
“The ascetic Gotama is repulsive; he teaches the Dhamma out of repulsiveness, and by that he trains his disciples.
“There is, Sīha, a way in which one who speaks rightly of me might say:
‘The ascetic Gotama is a remover; he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of removal, and by that he trains his disciples.’”
There is, Sīha, a way in which one speaking rightly might say of me:
"The ascetic Gotama is an ascetic; he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of asceticism, and by that he trains his disciples.
There is, Sīha, a way in which one speaking rightly might say of me: [and so forth].
“The ascetic Gotama is one who has transcended the womb; he teaches the Dhamma for the transcendence of the womb, and by that he trains his disciples.
“There is, Sīha, a way in which one speaking rightly could say of me:
‘The ascetic Gotama is one who has found consolation; he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of consolation, and by that he trains his disciples.’”
And what, Sīha, is the method by which one speaking rightly might say of me:
"The ascetic Gotama is a proponent of non-action; he teaches the Dhamma of non-action, and by that he trains his disciples"?
For I, Sīha, speak of the non-performance of bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct.
"I speak of the non-doing of manifold evil, unwholesome states.
This, Sīha, is the method by which one who speaks correctly of me might say:
'The ascetic Gotama is a proponent of non-doing; he teaches a doctrine of non-doing, and by means of that he trains his disciples.'"
And what, Sīha, is the method by which one speaking rightly might say of me:
“The ascetic Gotama is a proponent of action; he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of action, and by that he trains his disciples”?

For I, Sīha, proclaim action: I proclaim action in regard to good conduct of body, good conduct of speech, and good conduct of mind; I proclaim action in regard to the various kinds of wholesome states.
This, Sīha, is the method by which one speaking rightly might say of me:
"The ascetic Gotama is an advocate of action; he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of action, and by that he trains his disciples.
And what, Sīha, is the method by which one speaking rightly might say of me?
“Does the ascetic Gotama hold the doctrine of annihilation? Does he teach the Dhamma for the sake of annihilation, and does he train his disciples thereby?
“I do indeed, Sīha, speak of the annihilation of lust, hatred, and delusion;
I speak of the annihilation of manifold kinds of evil, unwholesome states.”
This, Sīha, is the way in which one speaking rightly might say of me:
"The ascetic Gotama is an annihilationist; he teaches a doctrine of annihilation and trains his disciples therein.
And what, Sīha, is the way in which one speaking rightly might say of me?
"Do you claim that the ascetic Gotama is one who feels disgust, teaches the Dhamma out of a sense of disgust, and trains his disciples by means of that disgust?
"Indeed, Sīha, I feel disgust for bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct;
I feel disgust at the attainment of various kinds of evil, unwholesome states."
This, Sīha, is the method by which one speaking correctly of me might say:
"The ascetic Gotama is loathsome; he teaches the Dhamma out of loathsomeness, and by that he trains his disciples.
And what, Sīha, is the method by which one speaking correctly of me might say this?
"Is it true, Sīha, that the ascetic Gotama is a disciplinarian who teaches the Dhamma for the sake of discipline and trains his disciples by means of that?
"I do, Sīha, teach the Dhamma for the sake of discipline—for the sake of disciplining lust, hatred, and delusion.
I teach the Dhamma for the sake of disciplining various kinds of evil, unwholesome states."
This, Sīha, is the method by which one speaking correctly might say of me:
"The ascetic Gotama is a disciplinarian; he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of discipline, and by that he disciplines his disciples.
And what, Sīha, is the method by which one speaking correctly might say of me?
“Is it true, Sīha, that the ascetic Gotama is an ascetic who teaches the Dhamma for the sake of asceticism and trains his disciples by means of it?
“Sīha, I say that there are evil, unwholesome qualities that are to be heated up:
bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct.”

“Sīha, one for whom evil, unwholesome states that lead to remorse have been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that they are no more subject to future arising—him I call an ascetic.

Now, Sīha, such evil, unwholesome states that lead to remorse have been abandoned by the Tathāgata, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that they are no more subject to future arising.”
"This, Sīha, is the way in which one speaking rightly might say of me: 'The ascetic Gotama teaches the Dhamma for the sake of austerity and trains his disciples by means of that.
And what, Sīha, is the way in which one speaking rightly might say of me:
'The ascetic Gotama is one who has ended the womb; he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of ending the womb and trains his disciples by means of that'?"

"Sīha, for one who has abandoned the future lying in a womb, the production of renewed existence, uprooted it, made it like a palm stump, rendered it incapable of future arising, and brought it to a state of non-existence—I call him 'one beyond the womb.

Sīha, for the Tathāgata, the future lying in a womb, the production of renewed existence, has been abandoned, uprooted, made like a palm stump, rendered incapable of future arising, and brought to a state of non-existence.
This, Sīha, is the method by which one speaking rightly would speak of me."
“The ascetic Gotama is one who has transcended the womb; he teaches the Dhamma for the transcendence of the womb, and by that he trains his disciples.
And what, Sīha, is the method by which one speaking rightly would say of me:
“The ascetic Gotama is comforted; he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of comfort, and by that he trains his disciples”?
“For I, Sīha, am comforted by the supreme consolation; I teach the Dhamma for the sake of consolation, and by that I train my disciples.
This, Sīha, is the way in which one speaking rightly might say of me:
‘The ascetic Gotama is comforted and teaches the Dhamma for the sake of consolation, and by that he trains his disciples.’”
When this was said, Sīha the general said to the Blessed One:
“Magnificent, Bhante!
… [as before] … May the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life shall last.”
“Investigate thoroughly, Sīha; thorough investigation is good for well-known people such as yourself.

“By this, Bhante, I am even more satisfied and delighted with the Blessed One because the Blessed One has said to me:

24. The Account of Roja the Mallan.
Then the Blessed One, having stayed at Āpaṇa for as long as he pleased, set out on a walking tour toward Kusinārā together with a great community of monks, numbering twelve hundred and fifty monks.
The Mallas of Kusinārā heard: “The Blessed One, it is said, is coming to Kusinārā together with a great community of monks, numbering twelve hundred and fifty monks.
They made a covenant: “Whosoever does not go out to meet the Blessed One shall be fined five hundred [pieces of money].”
Now at that time, Roja the Mallian was a friend of the Venerable Ānanda.
Then the Blessed One, wandering by stages on his tour, arrived at Kusinārā.
Thereupon, the Mallas of Kusinārā went out to meet the Blessed One.
Then Roja the Mallian, having gone out to meet the Blessed One, approached the Venerable Ānanda; having approached, he paid homage to the Venerable Ānanda and stood to one side.
As he was standing there, the Venerable Ānanda said this to Roja the Mallian:
"It is a sublime thing for you, friend Roja, that you have come out to meet the Blessed One."
“Venerable Ānanda, it was not out of great devotion to the Buddha, the Dhamma, or the Saṅgha that I did this;
rather, a compact was made with my kinsmen: ‘Whoever does not go out to meet the Blessed One shall be fined five hundred pieces.
It was only out of fear of that fine from my kinsmen, venerable Ānanda, that I went out to meet the Blessed One.”
Then the Venerable Ānanda was displeased, thinking, "How indeed can Roja the Mallian speak thus?
Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
Sitting to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, this Roja the Mallian is a well-known person of renown.
Indeed, such well-known persons as these stand to gain great benefit from having confidence in this Dhamma and Discipline.
It would be well, venerable sir, if the Blessed One were to act in such a way that Roja the Mallian might gain confidence in this Dhamma and Discipline.”
“Ānanda, it was not difficult for the Tathāgata that Roja the Mallian should gain confidence in this Dhamma and Discipline.
Then the Blessed One, having suffused Roja the Mallian with a mind of loving-kindness, rose from his seat and entered his dwelling.
Then Roja the Mallian, touched by the Blessed One’s mind of loving-kindness—just like a young calf [touching] its mother—[approached the Blessed One].
In this very manner, having approached dwelling after dwelling and courtyard after courtyard, he asked the bhikkhus:
"Venerable sirs, where does the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, dwell at present? For we wish to see that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
"Friend Roja, that dwelling has its door closed. Approach it quietly and without haste; enter the porch, clear your throat, and knock on the bolt. The Blessed One will open the door for you."

Then Roja the Mallian approached that monastery, which had its doors closed; approaching quietly and unhurriedly, he entered the porch, cleared his throat, and knocked on the bolt. The Blessed One opened the door.
Then Roja the Mallian entered the monastery, paid homage to the Blessed One, and sat down to one side.
As Roja the Mallian was sitting there, the Blessed One gave him a progressive discourse, namely:
After the discourse on giving...

25. The Story of Those Who Went Forth in Old Age.
Then the Blessed One, having stayed at Kusinārā for as long as he pleased, set out on a wandering tour toward Ātumā together with a great community of monks, numbering twelve hundred and fifty monks.
Now at that time, a certain man who had gone forth in old age was residing at Ātumā; he had previously been a barber.
He had two sons who were sweet-voiced and eloquent, skillful and perfectly trained in their own ancestral craft of barbering.
That elder who had gone forth heard: "The Blessed One, it is said, is coming to Ātumā together with a great Saṅgha of monks, numbering twelve hundred and fifty monks.
Then that elder who had gone forth said this to those boys:
"Sons, the Blessed One, it is said, is coming to Ātumā together with a great Saṅgha of monks, numbering twelve hundred and fifty monks."
“Go, dear ones, take your baskets and travel from house to house with a measuring ladle;
collect salt, oil, rice, and hard food, so that we may prepare a drink of conjey for the Blessed One when he arrives.”

“Very well, dear ones,” those boys replied to that elder who had gone forth, and taking their barber’s kit, they went from house to house with a small measure-bag, collecting salt, oil, rice, and hard food.
Seeing those boys, who were so charming and eloquent, even those people who did not wish to have work done were made to do it; and having had it done, they gave them much.
Then those boys gathered together much salt, oil, rice, and solid food.
Then the Blessed One, traveling by stages on his journey, arrived at Ātumā.
There, the Blessed One stayed at Ātumā in the Bhusāgāra (the House of Dung).
Then, at the end of that night, that elder who had gone forth into homelessness had plenty of rice-gruel prepared and offered it to the Blessed One, saying:
"Venerable sir, may the Blessed One accept my rice-gruel.
Although Tathāgatas know [the answer], they ask; ... [as before] ...

Then the Blessed One said this to that elder who had gone forth late in life:
"Monk, where is this rice-gruel?"
Then that one who had gone forth in old age reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked him:
"It is unbecoming, foolish man, it is unsuitable, it is unworthy, it is unbefitting for a recluse, it is improper, and it is not to be done."
"How indeed, foolish man, can you, having gone forth, encourage others in what is unallowable?
This, foolish man, will not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
Having rebuked him and given a discourse on the Dhamma, he addressed the monks:"
“Monks, one who has gone forth should not encourage others in what is improper; whoever should so encourage them, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
Furthermore, monks, one who was formerly a barber should not carry a barber’s kit;
whoever should carry one, there is an offense of wrong-doing.”
Then the Blessed One, having stayed at Ātumā for as long as he pleased, set out on a wandering tour toward Sāvatthī.
Traveling by stages on his tour, he arrived at Sāvatthī.
There the Blessed One dwelt at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, much fruit and fresh food had been produced in Sāvatthī.
Then it occurred to the monks:
"What, indeed, has been permitted by the Blessed One regarding fruit and fresh food, and what has not been permitted?"
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, all kinds of fruits and fresh foods,” he said.
Now at that time, seeds belonging to the Saṅgha were being planted on land belonging to an individual, and seeds belonging to an individual were being planted on land belonging to the Saṅgha.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“Monks, seeds belonging to the Saṅgha that have been planted on land belonging to an individual may be used after giving a portion [to the owner].
Seeds belonging to an individual that have been planted on land belonging to the Saṅgha may be used after giving a portion [to the Saṅgha].”
26. The Discourse on the Four Great References Now at that time, anxiety arose among the bhikkhus regarding various matters:
"What has been permitted by the Blessed One? What has not been permitted?"
They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“Monks, whatever I have not prohibited by saying, ‘This is not allowable,’ if it conforms to what is unallowable and contradicts what is allowable, that is not allowable for you.
Monks, whatever I have not prohibited by saying, ‘This is not allowable,’ if it conforms to what is allowable and contradicts what is unallowable, that is allowable for you.”
“Monks, whatever has not been authorized by me as ‘this is allowable,’ if it conforms to what is unallowable and opposes what is allowable, that is not allowable for you.
Whatever has not been authorized by me as ‘this is allowable,’ if it conforms to what is allowable and opposes what is unallowable, that is allowable for you.
Then, it occurred to the monks:
“Is it allowable to use what is for the time being with what is for the watch of the night, or is it not allowable?
Is it allowable to use what is for the time being with what is for seven days, or is it not allowable?
Is it allowable to use what is for the time being with what is for as long as life lasts, or is it not allowable?”
“Is it allowable to use what is for a watch of the night with what is for seven days, or is it not allowable?
Is it allowable to use what is for a watch of the night with what is for as long as life lasts, or is it not allowable?
Is it allowable to use what is for seven days with what is for as long as life lasts, or is it not allowable?”
They reported this matter to the Blessed One:

“Monks, when a *yāmakālika* (medicinal substance to be used during the watch of the night) is received on the same day as a *yāvakālika* (medicinal substance to be used during the day), it is allowable at the proper time, but not allowable at the improper time.

Monks, when a *sattāhakālika* (medicinal substance to be used for seven days) is received on the same day as a *yāvakālika*, it is allowable at the proper time, but not allowable at the improper time.”
“Monks, that which is for life may be received on the day it is given; it is allowable at the proper time, but not allowable at the improper time.
Monks, that which is for seven days may be received on the day it is given; it is allowable during the watch [of the night], but when the watch has passed, it is not allowable.
Monks, that which is for life may be received on the day it is given; it is allowable during the watch, but when the watch has passed, it is not allowable.”
